text: Adapting large language models under GPU memory limits requires balancing weights, optimizer states, gradients, and activations.
This note evaluates LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, LongLoRA, and QA-LoRA.
We separate architectural designs from measured benchmarks, evaluate an unverified laboratory claim, and specify a controlled experimental protocol.
Full fine-tuning stores 16 bytes per parameter under Adam.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) freezes base weights, eliminating optimizer memory for the backbone.

Low-Rank Adaptation establishes factorized tuning: LoRA freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks. In benchmarked evaluations: Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times. This reduction is specific to 175B parameters; it cannot be transferred to 7B models where activations dominate peak VRAM.

Adaptive Low-Rank Adaptation dynamically allocates rank across layers: AdaLoRA parameterizes the incremental updates in the form of singular value decomposition. Pruning minor singular values yields high efficiency: For example, AdaLoRA achieves 88.7% F1 on SQuADv2.0 with the smallest budget 0.08%.

Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation isolates magnitude and direction: DoRA decomposes the pre-trained weight into two components, magnitude and direction, for fine-tuning, specifically employing LoRA for directional updates to efficiently minimize the number of trainable parameters. Detaching the directional norm eliminates backpropagation overhead: The results indicate that the modification leads to a training memory reduction of approximately 24.4% in fine-tuning LLaMA and 12.4% in VL-BART.

text: Quantized adaptation targets 16-bit base weights.

section: Base Model Quantization and Activation Scaling
text: QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters. Utilizing 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), double quantization, and paged optimizers: QLoRA reduces the average memory requirements of finetuning a 65B parameter model from >780GB of GPU memory to <48GB without degrading the runtime or predictive performance compared to a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline.

section: Base Model Quantization and Activation Scaling
text: To avoid quantization error during low-bit deployment: QA-LoRA addresses the issue by introducing group-wise operators which increase the degree of freedom of low-bit quantization and decrease that of LoRA. This enables direct INT4 matrix fusion: Additionally, during the inference stage, QA-LoRA is also more than 50% faster than QLoRA because the fine-tuned model (after weight integration) is still in INT4, unlike QLoRA that converts it back to FP16.

section: Base Model Quantization and Activation Scaling
text: In addition to training LoRA weights in linear layers, LongLoRA further makes embedding and normalization layers trainable. Utilizing Shifted Sparse Attention (S2-Attn): LongLoRA closes the accuracy gap that between conventional LoRA and full fine-tuning, while still maintaining up to 1.8× lower memory cost than full fine-tuning.
Selecting an adaptation strategy requires balancing parameter savings, activations, and deployment latency.

An informal laboratory assertion claims: ``Our pilot halves training memory compared with LoRA.'' This statement is entirely unverified: Our pilot halves training memory compared with LoRA.
No technical specification, log, batch size, or sequence length was provided to substantiate it.
On a 7B model with 16-bit LoRA, base weights consume ≈14 GB, while adapter states take <150 MB.
With gradient checkpointing, base weights dominate over 80% of allocated VRAM.
Halving total training memory cannot occur through adapter reparameterization alone; it strictly requires 4-bit base quantization, offloading, or sequence truncation.
Hence, this claim is rejected as an empirical finding and excluded from experimental planning.
To establish rigorous memory and throughput boundaries, we specify a controlled benchmark on a 24 GB GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4090).
We evaluate LLaMA-3-8B across four conditions: 16-bit LoRA, 4-bit QLoRA (NF4), 16-bit DoRA, and 4-bit QA-LoRA (INT4) (r=16, =32 across attention and MLP projections).

All runs enforce identical AdamW settings (1=0.9, 2=0.999, =10-8, weight decay 0.0), a cosine schedule (2 × 10-4 to 2 × 10-5 with 3% warmup), and fixed seed 42 for shuffling, initialization, and dropout.
We fix effective batch size strictly at 16 across all runs via per-device batch size 2 and 8 accumulation steps (2 × 8 = 16).
Training uses 10,000 Alpaca examples under sequence lengths L \512, 2048, 4096 evaluated with and without gradient checkpointing.

Telemetry distinguishes peak allocated VRAM (active tensors via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated) from peak reserved VRAM (caching allocator overhead and fragmentation via torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved).
Step throughput is logged in tokens per second.
Downstream accuracy is evaluated on 5-shot MMLU and ARC-Challenge; inference latency is profiled across batch sizes 1 to 8.
Several methodological boundaries govern this note.

Reported memory savings and training speedups from published benchmarks cannot be assumed to generalize across differing model architectures, sequence lengths, batch sizes, or GPU hardware without direct empirical measurement.
Specifically, 4-bit dequantization latency depends heavily on Tensor Core support and GPU memory bandwidth.
Shifted Sparse Attention requires rotary position embeddings and does not transfer to absolute position encodings without adaptation.
Finally, published metrics cited here were verified against archival sources, whereas informal laboratory assertions remain strictly unverified.
